statement:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with non-parallel sides $BC$ and $AD$. Assume that there is a point $E$ on the side $BC$ such that the quadrilaterals $ABED$ and $AECD$ are circumscribed. Prove that there is a point $F$ on the side $AD$ such that the quadrilaterals $ABCF$ and $BCDF$ are circumscribed if and only if
\[
AB\parallel CD.
\]
solutions: Let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be the incircles of the tangential quadrilaterals $ABED$ and $AECD$, and let their centers be $O_1$ and $O_2$, respectively. Let the tangent from $B$ to $\omega_2$ other than $BC$ meet $AD$ at $F_1$, and let the tangent from $C$ to $\omega_1$ other than $BC$ meet $AD$ at $F_2$. If a point $F$ has the required property, then $\omega_1$ must also be the incircle of $ABCF$, so $CF$ is the second tangent from $C$ to $\omega_1$ and therefore $F=F_2$. Similarly, $\omega_2$ must be the incircle of $BCDF$, so $BF$ is the second tangent from $B$ to $\omega_2$ and $F=F_1$. Conversely, if $F_1=F_2$, the two circles are incircles of the required quadrilaterals. Hence it is enough to prove \[ F_1=F_2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad AB\parallel CD. \tag{1} \] Let \[ O=AD\cap BC. \] The circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are tangent to both sides of the angle formed by the lines $AD$ and $BC$. Put \[ p=OO_1\cdot OO_2. \] We use the following lemma. \textbf{Lemma.} Two circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$, with centers $O_1,O_2$, are inscribed in an angle with vertex $O$. Points $P,S$ lie on one side of the angle and $Q,R$ on the other. Suppose that $\omega_1$ is the incircle of triangle $PQO$, while $\omega_2$ is the excircle of triangle $RSO$ opposite $O$. Then exactly one of the following holds: \[ OP\cdot ORp>OQ\cdot OS, \] or \[ OP\cdot OR=p=OQ\cdot OS. \tag{2} \] \textbf{Proof of the lemma.} Let \[ \angle OPO_1=u, \quad \angle OQO_1=v, \quad \angle OO_2R=x, \quad \angle OO_2S=y, \quad \angle POQ=2\varphi. \] Because the indicated lines are internal or external angle bisectors in triangles $PQO$ and $RSO$, \[ u+v=x+y=90^\circ-\varphi. \tag{3} \] By the sine rule, \[ \frac{OP}{OO_1}=\frac{\sin(u+\varphi)}{\sin u}, \qquad \frac{OO_2}{OR}=\frac{\sin(x+\varphi)}{\sin x}. \] Since $u,x,\varphi$ are acute, \[ \begin{aligned} OP\cdot OR\ge p &\Longleftrightarrow \frac{OP}{OO_1}\ge\frac{OO_2}{OR}\\ &\Longleftrightarrow \sin x\sin(u+\varphi)\ge \sin u\sin(x+\varphi)\\ &\Longleftrightarrow \sin(x-u)\ge 0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow x\ge u. \end{aligned} \tag{4} \] Equality holds exactly when $x=u$. Analogously, \[ p\ge OQ\cdot OS \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v\ge y, \tag{5} \] with equality exactly when $v=y$. By (3), the inequalities $x\ge u$ and $v\ge y$ are equivalent, and equality in one is equivalent to equality in the other. This proves (2). \hfill$\square$ We now apply the lemma three times. First use the tangent lines $ED$ to $\omega_1$ and $BF_1$ to $\omega_2$. The lemma compares the products \[ OB\cdot OD \qquad\text{and}\qquad OE\cdot OF_1. \] Thus \[ OE\cdot OF_1>p \quad\Longrightarrow\quad OB\cdot ODp. \tag{7} \] Third, interchange the roles of the two circles and use the tangent lines $AE$ and $CF_2$. The lemma compares \[ OA\cdot OC \qquad\text{and}\qquad OE\cdot OF_2. \] Thus (7) implies \[ OE\cdot OF_2p>OE\cdot OF_2, \] so $F_1\ne F_2$.
